name: Guinea-Bissau
summary: A Portuguese colony that won independence (declared 1973, recognised 1974) after a war led by Amílcar Cabral’s PAIGC; frequent coups since.

location.value: West Africa on the Atlantic; 36,125 km².

terrain.value: Low coastal swamps, mangroves and river estuaries, with the Bijagós archipelago of about 80 islands offshore.

climate.value: Tropical, with a hot, humid rainy season (June–October) and a dry season.

resources.value: Cashew nuts (the main export), fish, rice, timber and unexploited bauxite and phosphate.

disasters.value: Floods in the rainy season, coastal erosion and droughts have hit farmers.

urbanisation.value: Bissau, the capital, is the only large city; most people live in villages.

disease.value: Malaria, cholera and tuberculosis are major diseases, and health care is limited.

migration.value: Many people have emigrated to Senegal, Portugal and France, and thousands fled during the 1998–99 war.

economicBase.value: Agriculture; fish, cashew nuts and groundnuts are the major exports.

tradeRoutes.value: Cashews and fish leave through the port of Bissau; much trade passes by road to Senegal.

wealth.value: HDI 0.514 (rated low, 174th, 2023); GDP per person and HDI are among the lowest in the world. The article does not use the term “low-income country”.

moneyAndTax.value: The West African CFA franc, shared with neighbours and pegged to the euro.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary semi-presidential republic; the infobox says it is under a military junta (2025).

keyRulers.value: Luís Cabral (president 1974–80), Amílcar Cabral’s half-brother, and João Bernardo Vieira, who took power in a 1980 coup and was killed in 2009.

succession.value: Coups and attempted coups have been frequent, so power seldom passes through peaceful elections.

institutions.value: Weak state institutions, a National People’s Assembly and a judiciary that often lacks independence.

stability.value: Coups in 1980 (João Bernardo Vieira, 14 November), 2012 (12 April) and 2025 (26 November).

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The armed forces grew out of the PAIGC guerrilla army and have often intervened in politics.

majorWars.value: The 1998–99 civil war followed an army uprising in May 1998; the president was ousted in June 1999.

territoryChange.value: The borders were drawn by France and Portugal in 1886 and have stayed unchanged.

alliancesRivals.value: A member of ECOWAS and of the Community of Portuguese-speaking Countries, with close ties to Portugal and Senegal.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Literacy is low, and schools and universities are few and under-funded.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: River boats and ferries link the islands and mainland, and roads are poor.

religion.value: About half are Muslim, a quarter are Christian, and many follow traditional beliefs.

languageWriting.value: Portuguese is official (about 2% first language); Guinea-Bissau Creole is the national language of unity.

artsArchitecture.value: Bijagós masks and carvings, gumbe music and Portuguese colonial buildings in Bissau.

socialStructure.value: Many ethnic groups, including the Balanta, Fula, Manjaco and Mandinka, with Kriol as a common language.

sharedIdentity.value: The armed struggle for independence (1963–74) is the main national symbol.

dailyLife.value: Most families farm rice and cashews in villages; rice with fish or palm oil sauce is the main meal.

neighbours.value: Senegal to the north and Guinea to the south and east.

colonisation.value: Portuguese Guinea, 1588–1974 (Portuguese presence from the 16th century); the Kaabu Empire 1537–1867.

riseSignals.value: Independence unilaterally declared on 24 September 1973; formally recognised on 10 September 1974.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: The military seized power on 26 November 2025; General Horta Inta-A (Na Man) has been transitional president since 27 November 2025.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
